name: Zane Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Zane. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and this is all confidential. Could you tell me what a normal day at work looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I'm on a dozer at the Barlow open cut, the coal mine east of town, and mostly I'm cleaning up the benches and pushing the spoil, the waste rock, over the edge after the trucks dump it. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off. I like that nobody talks to me for most of it. I don't like the new screen they put in the cab, it beeps at me when I'm off the plan by half a metre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on the dozer?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was thirty years at the sawmill in Harlan, on the log yard, until the mill shut when the big company bought it and moved everything south. I was fifty-five. Marlene does the books part-time at the hardware store, and between us we pay the bills and not much else. We've got maybe two or three weeks in the bank, no more. I'm still the guy the supervisor sends to the easy jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone was going on about it and nothing happened, like the year two thousand thing. I don't go online, so I'd say it at the break table and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I keep my job for now. The computer never scared me. What scares me is the boss with a calculator deciding a dozer can drive itself. That's a different thing and that's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, push dirt, try to get better on the steep benches so they stop giving me the easy stuff. Pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the boss with a calculator still worries you. Is there something specific going on at Barlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've got a remote dozer on the north side, run by a guy in a room in town. I hear it works about as well as I do, which isn't saying much. Nobody talks about it in front of us, which tells you something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home if things stayed like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Marlene wants a new fridge, the old one sounds like a tractor. Maybe next year. We're not big spenders, we can't be.

S0.say: He'd say 'I told you so' at the break table, comparing AI to past scares that came to nothing; he doesn't go online.
S0.think: He thinks it means keeping his job for now, but he's still worried about managers deciding a dozer can drive itself, which has nothing to do with clever AI.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and pushing dirt, trying to improve on the steep benches so he stops being given the easy jobs. Keeps paying the bills and maybe replaces the fridge next year.
S0.quote: The computer never scared me. What scares me is the boss with a calculator deciding a dozer can drive itself.
S0.fieldNote: Zane speaks in short, flat sentences and resists drama. Even in the calm picture he points to a remote dozer already working at Barlow, but he files it away as a separate, slower threat. His wishes are small and practical, like replacing a noisy fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, they'll do what makes money. I wouldn't make a big speech. I'd probably say 'let's see what happens' and go back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, dozers are going to be in the first lot. They've got one on the north side already. I'm the newest and the slowest on the dozers, so if they cut three, I'm one of the three, simple maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and hope they need some of us. We'd stop the fridge, stop eating out on Fridays, and Marlene would look for more hours. I wouldn't do any computer course, I'd just make it hard for them to say I'm bad at my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. More than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take a computer course. If the mine offered one with pay, would that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if they paid, I'd sit in the room. But I'd be wasting their time. I can't use the screen in my own cab without swearing at it. My grandson does my phone for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'let's see what happens' in public, but you've just told me you'd be one of the first three. Which is closer to how you really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second one. 'Let's see' is just what you say. You don't tell the guys you're scared, they'd never let you forget it. Marlene knows, that's enough.

S1.say: He'd say it's just business, companies will do what makes money, and he'd tell co-workers 'let's see what happens'.
S1.think: He believes dozers will be among the first jobs cut, and as the newest and slowest dozer driver he'd be one of the first to go.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and tries to look indispensable rather than retraining. Cuts the new fridge and Friday meals out while his wife looks for more hours.
S1.feel: Worried, more than he'd admit out loud.
S1.quote: I'm the newest and the slowest on the dozers, so if they cut three, I'm one of the three, simple maths.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between Zane's public 'let's see' and his private arithmetic that he'd be among the first cut. He won't consider retraining seriously and says so, preferring to make himself hard to fault. He doesn't blame anyone; he calls it business, which fits his middle-of-the-road outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's not much anyone can do, it's happening everywhere. Maybe I'd say the government should have seen it coming. I'm not a protest sort of guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be gone in a year and so would the mine as I know it. Sixty, no qualifications, a dozer driver who still gets the easy jobs. I've already watched one place shut with me in it. I didn't think I'd get a second go at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and ask about taking my pension early, even at the reduced rate, because some money is better than none. We'd sell the boat trailer and the second car. And we'd probably have to ask our daughter in the city if we could lean on her for a while, which I would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going. I don't really have another word for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, is there anything you'd try first, before going to the pension office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overtime, as much as they'd give me. Maybe ask around for driving work, but if robots are doing hands-on stuff, there's no driving either. Two years isn't long enough to learn anything, so I'd just work and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would asking your daughter for help look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marlene would ask, not me. Our daughter's a nurse, she's good, she'd say yes before we finished. I'd sit there feeling like I'd failed. My father never asked anyone for anything.

S2.say: He'd say there's not much anyone can do and that the government should have seen it coming, but he wouldn't protest.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be out within a year: sixty, no qualifications, and living through a closure for the second time.
S2.do: Asks about taking his pension early at a reduced rate and works all the overtime he can get. Sells the boat trailer and the second car, and leans on his daughter for help.
S2.feel: Like the floor is giving way.
S2.quote: I've already watched one place shut with me in it. I didn't think I'd get a second go at that.
S2.fieldNote: Zane's sawmill closure makes this picture feel personal, a 'second go' at watching a workplace shut. He doesn't look for any new path; he reaches for an early pension, overtime and family. His shame about asking his daughter for help, and his father's example, sit under the plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's business, but I'd add that five years gives people a chance. I'd tell the young guys to sort themselves out early. Me, I'd just say I'm hanging on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'm sixty-three. Close enough to see the end, not close enough to get there. If I can stretch it to sixty-three with a bit in the bank, I can probably stretch the rest with Marlene's hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly, a fixed amount every pay, even if it's small. We'd stop the little things now, not later: the takeaway, the cable TV. Otherwise I'd keep going and see if they keep a few drivers on till the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could live with it. It's a long slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the fixed amount every pay be, realistically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty, maybe fifty. That's about two and a half thousand a year, so ten-odd thousand by the time it comes. Not much, but it's a buffer for when the pension isn't there yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning the new systems at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I know I should. But I'm not going to be good at it, and they'd pick someone younger anyway. Better I'm a good dozer driver for five years than a bad screen watcher.

S3.say: He'd still call it business but say five years gives people a chance, advising younger workers to sort themselves out early while he hangs on.
S3.think: He thinks reaching sixty-three with some savings could let him bridge the rest of the way to his pension with his wife's earnings.
S3.do: Saves forty or fifty every pay and cuts takeaways and cable TV straight away. Keeps working and waits to see whether a few drivers are kept until the end.
S3.feel: A long, slow worry he can live with.
S3.quote: If I can stretch it to sixty-three with a bit in the bank, I can probably stretch the rest with Marlene's hours.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Zane build a small, sober plan, and he can do the maths out loud. He still won't retrain, preferring to be a good dozer driver over a bad screen watcher, which he admits he knows is not ideal. He remains in waiting mode, but with a purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, nobody knows what'll happen. I'd say it's a problem for the young ones. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'm sixty-eight, which means I'm out anyway, one way or another. Ten years, that's not my problem, that's my grandson's problem, and that bothers me more than I thought it would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep putting a bit aside, pay off the car. I'd tell my grandson not to bother with machine driving. Nothing much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly alright. A bit uneasy for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, that's the trouble. Not dozers, not trucks. Something with people, maybe, nursing like his mum. I'd tell him to listen to his mum, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it bothers you more than you thought. What is it exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I wouldn't be able to help him. My dad could tell me 'go to the mill', and that was that, a job for life. I'd have nothing to tell the boy.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time, nobody knows what will happen, and it's a problem for younger people.
S4.think: He thinks he'll be out of work anyway at sixty-eight, and that the real problem belongs to his grandson, which bothers him more than he expected.
S4.do: Keeps working, keeps saving a little and pays off the car. Tells his grandson not to go into machine driving.
S4.feel: Mostly alright, a bit uneasy for the younger ones.
S4.quote: Ten years, that's not my problem, that's my grandson's problem, and that bothers me more than I thought it would.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Zane is mostly safe in his own reckoning, but he is struck by having no advice to give his grandson. The contrast with his father pointing him to the mill was the most emotional moment in the interview. His actions stay minimal and steady.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. You'd have no time and no money and the pension isn't there yet. What would help is being able to take the pension early without losing a big chunk of it, for guys over fifty-five who get pushed out. That, and somebody to do the forms for you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask why they hire old guys like me if they're only going to get rid of us. I came here because the mill shut. If the mine shuts too, there's nowhere left to come to. That's this town in one sentence.

headlineQuote: I came here because the mill shut. If the mine shuts too, there's nowhere left to come to.
portrait: Zane Schmidt is 58 and drives a dozer at the Barlow open-cut coal mine, a job he took three years ago after thirty years on a sawmill log yard ended when the mill closed. He has two or three weeks of savings, a wife who keeps books part-time, and no taste for screens or computer courses. He calls automation 'business' rather than blaming anyone, says 'let's see' in public, and privately works out that he'd be among the first cut. The two-year picture brings back the mill closure, and his answer is an early pension and help from his daughter. With five or ten years he saves small, fixed amounts, and the long picture worries him mostly for his grandson.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no time, no money and no pension yet.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to take his pension early without losing a big part of it if he's pushed out after fifty-five, and someone to help with the forms.
